title: Write a `Predicate<Employee>` that checks salary > 50,000, then combine it with another predicate (department == "IT") using `.and()`.
shortTitle: Write a Predicate<Employee> for salary > 50000 and combine with department == "IT" using .and()

s1_definition.profdef: `Predicate<T>` is a functional interface returning a boolean test. Its default method `.and(other)` composes two predicates into one that is true only when both are true, with short-circuit evaluation and the first predicate tested first.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants employees who both earn above fifty thousand and work in IT. She writes two simple checks and glues them with "and", so only people passing both checks are selected.
s1_definition.oneliner: `highSalary.and(inIT)` is true only when both predicates pass, short-circuiting if the first fails.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Predicate<T>` is a functional interface returning a boolean test. Its default method `.and(other)` composes two predicates into one that is true only when both are true, with short-circuit evaluation and the first predicate tested first.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants employees who both earn above fifty thousand and work in IT. She writes two simple checks and glues them with "and", so only people passing both checks are selected.

**One line to remember:** `highSalary.and(inIT)` is true only when both predicates pass, short-circuiting if the first fails.

sections.s2_technical:
A `Predicate<Employee>` wraps a boolean test, for example `Predicate<Employee> highSalary = e -> e.getSalary() > 50_000`. Another predicate `Predicate<Employee> inIT = e -> "IT".equals(e.getDepartment())`. The default method `.and` combines them: `highSalary.and(inIT)` returns a new predicate true only when both hold.

`.and` short-circuits — if the first predicate is false, the second is never evaluated — and it tests the receiver predicate first, so ordering can matter for performance when one check is cheaper. Predicate also offers `.or` for either-true and `.negate` for inversion, letting you build complex filters declaratively.

The senior nuance is composing predicates for reuse and readability: each simple predicate has a clear name and can be tested and combined independently, which is far cleaner than one giant boolean expression. For performance I put the cheaper or more selective predicate first so short-circuiting eliminates most elements early. Composition turns filtering rules into named, reusable building blocks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A report at the National Bank of India must list employees who both earn more than fifty thousand and belong to the IT department, and the two conditions are reused separately elsewhere.

This is exactly what Predicate composition does — two named predicates combined with and produce the combined filter while remaining independently reusable.

The code defines an `EmployeeFilterService` with the two predicates and their combination.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh IT 1,000,000, Amit IT 40,000, Priya Sales 250,000, Karan IT 80,000.

Step 1: The combined predicate highSalary and inIT tests each employee.

Step 2: Rajesh passes both — high salary and IT — so he is kept.

Step 3: Amit fails highSalary, so and short-circuits and drops him; Priya passes highSalary but fails inIT and is dropped.

Step 4: Karan passes both and is kept, leaving Rajesh and Karan.

```
INFO: High-paid IT staff: [Rajesh, Karan]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  [Rajesh/IT/1M, Amit/IT/40k, Priya/Sales/250k, Karan/IT/80k]
    │ filter(highSalary.and(inIT))
    │ Rajesh: >50k & IT → keep
    │ Amit:   >50k → short-circuit → drop
    │ Priya:  >50k & IT → drop
    │ Karan:  >50k & IT → keep
    ▼
  [Rajesh, Karan]
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Composable Filter Rules ═══

  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────────────┐ ──names──→ Report
  │ staff    │→│ EmployeeFilterService│
  │ list     │ │ highSalary.and(inIT) │
  └──────────┘ └──────────────────────┘
     each predicate is a reusable, named building block
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Predicate composition ═══

  ┌─ default methods ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Predicate<T> test(T): boolean                              │
  │ .and(other) → true iff BOTH; short-circuits on first false │
  │ .or(other)  → true if either; .negate() → invert          │
  │ receiver tested FIRST → order cheap/selective check first  │
  │ named predicates = reusable, testable building blocks      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │      EmployeeFilterService    │
  │  - highSalary: Predicate       │ e -> salary > 50000
  │  - inIT: Predicate             │ e -> "IT".equals(dept)
  │  + highPaidIT(List): List      │ filter(highSalary.and(inIT))
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. stream().filter(highSalary.and(inIT))
  2. map(getName).toList()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Predicate is a functional interface that wraps a boolean test, and I define two simple ones: high salary checks that pay exceeds fifty thousand, and in IT checks that the department equals IT. The default method and composes them into a new predicate that is true only when both hold, so high salary dot and of in IT selects employees who satisfy both conditions at once.

Two behaviours of and matter. It short-circuits, so if the first predicate is false the second is never evaluated, and it tests the receiver predicate first, which means ordering affects performance when one check is cheaper or more selective. At the National Bank of India I put the more selective predicate first so most elements are eliminated early.

The senior point I stress is composition for reuse. Each simple predicate has a clear name, can be unit-tested on its own, and can be combined with and, or, and negate to build complex filters declaratively. That is far cleaner and more maintainable than one giant boolean expression inside a filter, because the same high-salary or in-IT predicate can be reused across many reports as a named building block.
